   Singapore banks fall ahead of earnings release; OCBC leads bank losses as STI slides 1.4%

 The slide comes ahead of the banks’ upcoming third quarter earnings announcements in early November.

 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise 中文 Singapore banks fell before third-quarter earnings, with OCBC down 3.7%, DBS 2.5% and UOB 2.2%. Great Eastern’s 72% profit drop hit OCBC hardest.
 The losses dragged the Straits Times Index down 1.4% to 5,303.84 by noon. UOB reports on Nov 4, then DBS on Nov 5 and OCBC on Nov 6.
 Analysts expect softer wealth fees and pressure on net interest margins. They will also watch AI-linked lending, bond yields, and bank capital strength.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – Shares of Singapore’s three local banks traded lower on the morning of Nov 2, with OCBC recording the steepest decline, ahead of their earnings releases in early November.
 As at 11.43 am, OCBC was down $1.07, or 3.7%, at $28.22, while DBS fell $1.82, or 2.5%, to $71.31. UOB declined 89 cents, or 2.2%, to $40.48.
 OCBC’s sharper decline came after its insurance subsidiary Great Eastern reported a 72% year-on-year fall in third-quarter net profit to $102.9 million on Nov 2, weighed down by weaker investment valuations and a one-off loss from the partial divestment of its Indonesian subsidiary.
 By noon, OCBC had extended its losses to trade at $28.26.
 Meanwhile, DBS and UOB pared some of their declines to $71.41 and $40.53, respectively.
 The losses among the banking heavyweights weighed on the benchmark Straits Times Index (STI), which was down 1.4%, or 72.9 points, at 5,303.84 as at noon.
 UOB will be the first to report its third-quarter earnings results on Nov 4, followed by DBS on Nov 5 and OCBC on Nov 6.
 Analysts had earlier told The Business Times that wealth management fees at Singapore banks could ease in the third quarter following a strong showing in the preceding three months, even as pressure on net interest margins persists.
 Investors are also expected to scrutinise the banks’ exposure to artificial intelligence-related financing and the impact of rising bond yields on their investment portfolios and capital positions.
 However, the analysts expect the banks’ underlying asset quality and capital positions to remain resilient. THE BUSINESS TIMES
